t: Akkadian, the oldest recorded Semitic language, was the language of the empires of Akkad, Babylon and Assyria, written in cuneiform for more than two and a half thousand years.
In the 2nd millennium BCE it was the international language of diplomacy, used in the letters exchanged between the pharaohs of Egypt and the kings of the Near East.

Its literature, from the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Babylonian creation epic to the laws of Hammurabi, and its records of astronomy, medicine and mathematics were recovered when scholars deciphered cuneiform in the 19th century.
dyk: In 1857 the Royal Asiatic Society sent copies of a newly found Assyrian inscription to four scholars, who translated it independently; their versions agreed so closely that the decipherment of Akkadian cuneiform was accepted as proved.
ev: Sargon of Akkad unites Mesopotamia and makes Akkadian a language of empire
Hammurabi of Babylon has his laws inscribed in Akkadian on stone stelae
The Amarna letters show Akkadian as the language of diplomacy between Egypt and the kingdoms of the Near East
Ashurbanipal gathers his library of cuneiform tablets at Nineveh
Cyrus the Great takes Babylon and records his conquest in Akkadian on the Cyrus Cylinder
The last datable cuneiform tablet, an astronomical almanac, is written at Uruk
Four scholars independently translate an Assyrian inscription, proving the decipherment
The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary is completed after nearly ninety years of work

f.family: Afroasiatic: the East Semitic branch of the Semitic languages
f.script: Cuneiform, taken over from the Sumerians, with signs for words and syllables
f.earliest: Akkadian names in Sumerian texts of about 2600 BCE; inscriptions of Sargon of Akkad, around 2300 BCE
f.status: Extinct: replaced by Aramaic as the spoken language in the 1st millennium BCE; written until the 1st century CE
